content.12.1.2 Ventricular arrhythmias: Ventricular arrhythmias can complicate and sometimes cause heart failure (HF). Frequent ventricular premature beats (VPBs/PVCs) may lead to reversible systolic dysfunction; factors include dyssynchrony and abnormal calcium handling. Initial management: correct precipitants (electrolyte abnormalities, hypo/hyperkalaemia, pro‑arrhythmic drugs), optimize HF drug therapy. Ischaemia may trigger arrhythmias but revascularization has not been shown to reduce risk. Amiodarone suppresses ventricular arrhythmias but does not reduce sudden cardiac death or overall mortality; may be considered for PVC‑induced cardiomyopathy to reduce recurrent arrhythmias and improve LV function, weighing side effects. Radiofrequency ablation of VPBs can improve LV function and possibly outcomes in tachycardiomyopathy when VPBs contribute to LV dysfunction; sustained reduction in PVC burden is associated with lower risk of cardiac mortality, transplant, or HF hospitalization.
content.12.1.3 Symptomatic bradycardia, pauses a: Pacemaker therapy indications in HF are similar to other cardiovascular disease. RV pacing may adversely affect LV systolic function and lead to HF. Patients with HFrEF needing frequent ventricular pacing (e.g., AV block or slow AF) and systolic dysfunction should receive CRT rather than a standard pacemaker to avoid adverse outcomes (BLOCK‑HF trial). Physiological pacing (e.g., His bundle pacing) is increasingly adopted as an alternative to RV pacing; nonrandomized data suggest fewer HF hospitalizations and a trend to reduced mortality, but more data are needed.
content.12.2 Chronic coronary syndromes: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the most common cause of HF across income settings and should be considered in all new-onset HF patients. Diagnostic workup for HF with chronic coronary syndromes (CCS) follows recent 2019 ESC Guidelines on CCS. Patients with HF should be carefully evaluated for signs/symptoms of CCS using history, family history, physical exam, ECG and imaging; documentation of ischaemia using non-invasive/invasive tests can be difficult in HF due to possible exercise intolerance.
